persona.bio: Nina, 36, ecommerce manager at a home goods brand. She runs the Shopify store: product pages, launches, discount codes, the email flows in Klaviyo, customer service escalations in Gorgias, and weekly sales numbers in Google Sheets. She writes product descriptions for every new item, plans promotions with the team over Gmail and Slack, and chases suppliers for images and specs. She uses ChatGPT and Claude every day. Her company encourages AI, and she can connect her work Gmail.

path.role: You’re the ecommerce manager at a home goods brand, running the Shopify store day to day.

steps.note: I am an ecommerce manager at a home goods brand, and I run our online store day to day. I write product descriptions, promo emails and replies to customers. My readers are shoppers deciding what to buy for their homes. I like a warm, clear and plain voice, with short sentences and no hype. Keep product copy to a short paragraph plus a few bullet free detail lines unless I say otherwise. Never add details I did not give you, like sizes, materials, finishes, prices or care claims. If something is missing, ask me or leave a square bracket. Do not make promises about shipping or returns.

steps.title: Your product descriptions, with a saved assistant
steps.read: Your product descriptions now live in a saved assistant in ChatGPT. It already knows your brand voice, your layout and what to avoid, so you only hand it the spec sheet and your notes. It keeps every listing sounding like the same store, and you read each one before it goes live.

material.label: Instructions for your assistant
items: You are my writing assistant for product descriptions. I am the ecommerce manager at a home goods brand and I run our Shopify store. Each time, I will give you a supplier spec sheet, my own notes, and sometimes old listing copy. Write a product description for our shoppers in a warm, clear, plain voice. Use short sentences. Start with one or two sentences on what the piece is and how it fits into a home. Then give a short list of key details: dimensions, materials, finish options and care, but only the ones I gave you. Never invent sizes, materials, certifications, prices or claims. If a detail is missing or unclear, list it at the end as a question for me. Avoid hype words and long adjective chains. Do not copy the supplier’s wording word for word. Give back the description, then the list of questions, and nothing else.

material.label: Examples to start with
items: Example 1. Oak nightstand. Details: [width] by [depth] by [height] inches, solid oak, finish options [finish 1] and [finish 2]. Description: A solid oak nightstand that sits neatly beside your bed. It has [number] drawer(s) for the things you reach for at night. Choose from [finish 1] or [finish 2] to suit your room. Details: [width] x [depth] x [height] inches. Solid oak. Wipe clean with a dry cloth.

Example 2. Ceramic planter. Details: [diameter] inches wide, [material], drainage hole [yes or no]. Description: A simple ceramic planter for your favorite plant. The [color] glaze gives it a soft, matte look on a shelf or windowsill. Details: [diameter] inches wide. [Drainage hole note]. Hand wash only.

Example 3. Linen throw blanket. Details: [size], [fabric], colors [colors]. Description: A soft linen throw to keep on the sofa or at the foot of the bed. It gets softer with each wash. Available in [colors]. Details: [size]. [Fabric]. Machine wash cold.

steps.title: Your customer replies, drafted in your inbox
steps.read: Your customer replies are drafted right inside Gmail with Help me write. Gmail drafts each reply and waits for your OK. You keep your own voice because you give it the point and then check every line before you send, which matters when a reply touches an order.

material.label: Starting lines for replies
items: Reply to [first name] with the dimensions and finish options for the [product name]. Say photos are attached or coming soon. Keep it friendly and short.
Tell [first name] that their order [order number] is being prepared and that I will send tracking when I have it. Thank them for waiting.
Thank [first name] for the question about [product name]. Say I am checking with our team and will reply by [day]. Keep it short.
Apologize to [first name] that the [product name] arrived [issue]. Ask for a photo and say I will follow up with next steps as soon as I check [our policy].
Tell [first name] that [product name] is out of stock right now and that I can [option, like notify them when it returns]. Keep it warm.
Answer [first name] about care for the [product name]. Use only this information: [care details]. Keep it plain.
Thank [first name] for their feedback on [product name]. Say I shared it with the team. Keep it two sentences.

material.label: Notes on your tone
items: Start with a plain, friendly draft. If it sounds stiff or too formal, press Friendly. If it sounds too casual for an upset customer or a formal request, press Formalize. If it runs long, press Shorten. If it adds a detail I did not give, like a date, price or policy, delete that line or fix it before sending. Always read the full draft and check the name, order details and any promise before I send it.

safeUse: Never type customer names, addresses, emails, phone numbers or order details into a chat tool. Use square brackets instead.
Do not paste payment details, account logins or anything from your store admin that is private.
Check every size, material, finish and care detail against the supplier spec sheet before a listing goes live.
Do not let AI state shipping, returns or warranty terms. Use your approved wording.
Read everything before it goes out, whether it is a listing, an email or a reply.
steps.askMessage: Hi [manager name], I use AI to help with my work as the ecommerce manager and I want to make sure I do it the right way. Which AI tools are approved here, and what may I use them for? I have in mind drafting product descriptions, updating listings, and drafting replies to customer messages in Gmail. I would also like to know if linking my work email to an AI tool is okay. I will keep customer details out of chat tools and read everything before it goes out.

design.today: You write these from spec sheets and notes, usually one a day. Details come from the supplier spec sheet, your own notes, photos you take and old listing copy.
design.newWay: A saved assistant in Claude holds your brand voice and your listing layout, so each new description starts as a draft built from the spec sheet and your notes. You paste in the material, read the draft, and fix any dimension, finish or material before it goes into Shopify. Every description comes out in the same shape, and you spend your effort on checking facts instead of starting from a blank page.

steps.goal: Get Claude ready on your phone and computer so you can use it wherever you work.
Pick three of your best existing listings and note what makes them sound like your brand.
Make a project for product descriptions and add your brand voice notes and your three best listings.
Set up the saved assistant so a pasted spec sheet and notes come back as a description in your usual layout.
Paste the checked description into the product page yourself.

When a message comes in, you paste it into your assistant, which drafts a reply from your saved answers and your product notes. You read it, fill any gap, and send it yourself, so replies sound like you and the facts stay right.

material.label: Reply guidance

material.label: Draft requests

design2.today: You pull weekly sales numbers into Sheets by hand.
